content: About order semantics, given that it's a huge part of the solution (I think the example solution grew like 150-200 lines because of it?.. not sure how long it was before that); I wonder what those who approved the puzzle already (@RunninglVlan and @NicknamedTwice) think about it? Should it be "find lexicographically the smallest build order", or a more natural but wordy "scan a digraph with dfs, visiting children in lexicographic order, with caching"?

Hey CodinGamer! Your contribution has unfortunately not been moderated on time and will temporarily be removed from the system... But no worries! You can republish it anytime to give it another chance! :)

Hello!

Build semantics seem to be quite complicated, and not written too clearly. From skimming the statement, I had two questions: (1) what needs to be built if the args line is empty, and (2) in what order do targets need to be built.

(1) is stated in the build semantics, but somewhere in the middle, not very visible; and the example makes it more confusing as it says "so the default target all is built" -- and one might thing (as I did) that the "all" target is the default one. It would be nice if you could put the actual rule somewhere more visible (though not sure where), or maybe if you rephrase the example to say something like "so the first target in the makefile, all, is built".

(2) however seems to be even less clear. Again, it was somewhat hard to find the line in build semantics that controlled this, and I don't think the conditions are sound, actually?

So you have two rules:
- Before a target is built, all of its prerequisites must be fully up to date
and
- When two targets can otherwise be built in any order, the one whose filename is lexicographically smaller is built first

However, if you have three targets, one being fully independent from two others, while those two depend on each other, say
A: C
B

Then according to the rules, C must be built after B, B must be built after A, and A must be built after C; which can't be properly ordered.

(This appears in the "Multiple action lines per rule" test, with "app", "docs" and "lib.o" for example.)

Am I missing something in the statement that resolves this ordering issue?


Edit: otherwise, this is a very interesting problem, I had fun trying to solve it :)

Hi! Thank you for trying the puzzle... I'm sorry you found the instructions unclear--I agree it is more complicated than most puzzles, and right on the edge of what works for CodinGame.  One problem I am bumping up against is the 5000 character limit for the problem statement--I'm right near the limit, so anything I add has to be balanced by removing something. Let me address your issues here:

(1) Yes, the relevant note is "If no required targets are explicitly given in cmdArgs, the first target in the first rule of the Makefile is the required target". I used to have more text about a default target, but after discussion with 5DN1L, we agreed on simplifying the vocabulary to just "required targets". My remaining sentence about "..., so the default target all is built." is confusing because its the only reference remaining to the term "default".  I can change that sentence to "Assume cmdArgs is empty, so the first target in the first rule (all) is built".  Would that help?

(2) You are correct that the rule "When two targets can otherwise be built in any order, the one whose filename is lexicographically smaller is built first" is ambiguous in the (reasonable) way you are interpreting it,  because the ordered sequence [C, A] is being compared to the independent sequence [B] and you are asked to decide which is lexicographically smaller.  The rule would be more clearly stated as "When either of two targets can otherwise be built next in the build order, the one whose filename is lexicographically smaller is built first."  Then it is clear that you are comparing "B" to "C" -- "A" is not eligible for consideration since it cannot be built yet.  With that rephrasing, is the build order clearer?

well most of the code growth was comments to help me remember what led to where it is... But your point is well-taken that making build order deterministic is just a detail to accommodate CodinGame's validation process, not something important for a makefile utility. 

I posed the question to Claude, and it proposed returning to the previous DFS with sorted children of a node, using the following description:

"For each target, its prerequisites are built one at a time, in lexicographic order of their names. A prerequisite must be completely built — including all of its own prerequisites, direct and indirect — before work on the next prerequisite begins. A target is built immediately after its last prerequisite is complete. A target that has already been built (or is already up-to-date) is not built again."

That basically forces a DFS implementation without explicitly saying as much...

How do you feel about that as an ordering rule?

It's your decision, both orderings make sense to me. I'd say it's a matter of how clearly it's described; the text snippet you provided above is kinda vague, and also it doesn't answer the question of what happens if multiple targets are requested to be built (are they iterated through in lexicographic order too, or in the order that they were specified?). "lexicographically smallest build order" is nice because it doesn't depend on the dependency graph structure, only the dependency relationship; at the same time "DFS walk (w/caching)" is probably a bit more natural for a makefile-like utility, and likely would result in a somewhat more efficient implementation (thought not that it matters much at the scale of the tests).

Hello, thank for the reply!

(1) Yes, that reads less confusing. (Makes sense about the character limit, yeah.)

(2) That doesn't really addressing the ordering issue. "can be built next in the build order", what would that even mean? The reasoning you provide of A and B not being comparable doesn't make sense, since if you want a unique linear order, any two objects should be comparable. Moreover, if you follow the (first) "Multiple action lines per rule" test with a similar situation with release: app docs,  app: lib.o ...;  the solution assumes it's being built in the order of lib.o -> app -> docs (-> release), even though docs and lib.o could in theory be built near each other (they are independent), and then docs should've been the first one to be built.

It seems that the actual order is obtained through a recursive dfs-like process of going through dependencies in lexicographical ordering + caching them if needed; and I'm not sure that there is a good way to specify the order among independent targets without specifying the whole "scanning" process.

As an example, if you have the following rules:

A: X Y
X: C
Y: B

you'll get order of C X B Y A

but if you just add a transitive dependencies from X and Y to A:

A: X Y B C
X: C
Y: B

you'll get an order of B C X Y A

even though no information about actual dependencies changed

Hmm… by “next in build order”, I mean: one way to solve the problem, abstractly, is to maintain a list of targets that are ready to build (all their prerequisites have been built), adding new targets to the list when they become ready, and removing targets from the list after they are built. The solution is just building one target at a time from the list until the list is empty. The lexicographic ordering convention just ensures a deterministic choice of which target in the list to build next. 

I’m happy to try to rephrase the lexicographic constraint in a way that is clearer if I can, without spelling out a specific algorithm since that is the core essence of the puzzle…

> maintain a list of targets that are ready to build
This wouldn't match the example solution though, for the example above you'd have

need to build: A, B, C, X, Y
ready: B, C
-> B
ready: C, Y
-> C
ready: X, Y
-> X
ready: Y
-> Y
ready: A
-> A

and you get order B C X Y A (regardless of whether you add B C to prerequisites of A directly or not).

The example solution would produce C X B Y A instead.

One rule that seems less important is that duplicate prerequisites (and targets) can be present in one rule, which means you need to remove some of them for $< macro. But it doesn't take up that much space either.

Finally, here's my solution to the puzzle :) Again, had fun solving it, so thanks for creating it :)


from collections import defaultdict
from functools import cmp_to_key

files = {(l:=input().split())[0]: int(l[1]) for _ in range(int(input()))}
args = {*input().split()}

act, dep, rdep = defaultdict(list), defaultdict(set), defaultdict(set)
T, R = [], []

for line in (input() for _ in range(int(input()))):
    line = line[:line.index('#') if '#' in line else len(line)]  # ignore comments
    if not line.strip(): continue  # ignore empty lines
    if line[:1] != '\t':  # rule
        T, R = [sorted(set(l:=s.split()), key=l.index) for s in line.split(':', 1)]  # ignore duplicates
        if not args: args = {T[0]}  # by default build the first target of the first rule
        t = set.union({*T}, *(rdep[x] for x in T))
        r = set.union({*R}, *( dep[x] for x in R))
        if t & r: exit(print('[Circular dependencies detected]'))
        for x in t: dep[x] |= r
        for x in r: rdep[x] |= t
    else:  # action
        for t in T:
            act[t].append([e for x in line.split() for e in {'$^': R, '$<': R[:1], '$@': [t]}.get(x, [x])])

for x in sorted(files, key=files.get):
    if dep[x] - {*files} or dep[x] and files[x] <= max(files[y] for y in dep[x]): # outdated
        del files[x]

args |= {x for x, v in rdep.items() if v & args}  # include dependencies
args -= {*files}  # cached files
_cmp = lambda x, y: [1, -1][x in dep[y] or y not in dep[x] and max({x}|dep[x]-dep[y]&args) < max({y}|dep[y]-dep[x]&args)]
[print(*l) for x in sorted(args, key=cmp_to_key(_cmp)) for l in act[x]]
print('[Build complete]')

You seem to have some insight into why the submission process can take so long. I've been wondering about that myself, as even very simple updates to straightforward puzzles can take quite a while and sometimes still end up failing with an error. That really shouldn't be happening. If you have any idea what's causing it, it'd be great if you could share your insights with the CG team; it might help them identify and fix the underlying issue.

Yes, I’ve been building a command line tool to help with managing, debugging, and submitting puzzles and contributions—I will share it when it is stable

The problem is definitely due to the fact that there is a single api for updating a contribution, and it does not return until every single test case (both local user tests and server validator tests) has been run against your reference solution and are confirmed to pass. The api fails if your tests don’t pass. 

Running a test server side is pretty heavyweight, it has to create a sandbox (a docker container or VM) with the right language support, inject your solution, compile and launch  your solution, and read the results. It seems slower for updating a contribution than submitting a puzzle solution—for one thing there are twice as many tests to run, but it may also be true that once a contribution is approved, the validation sandbox for the puzzle is persisted/optimized so it can spin up more quickly. 

The right solution to the timeout problem is to break the api into two parts—the first one would start the contribution update and put it into a pending state and return immediately. There would be a second api to poll for completion of the update and success/failure. That would solve the current timeout problem. Note that is already the way puzzle submission works, so they obviously know about the underlying problem. 

That wouldn’t speed up the time required to update a contribution, but it would eliminate the timeout problem. To speed it up, the simplest thing they could do is run all the tests in parallel. They may have considered that idea and rejected it because it causes brief bursts of increased resource usage (CPU and RAM). It’s also reasonable that optimizing the contribution experience isn’t at the top of their priority list, since the vast majority of users don’t make contributions.

* If I only change metadata (for example, the statement, test case names or ordering), the update completes almost immediately.

* If I modify only some of the test cases, only those cases are revalidated.

These observations suggest that the backend is already smart enough to avoid rerunning validation when it isn't necessary, and to revalidate only the affected cases. That said, even updating a single test case can still fail due to the timeout.

I’m happy to have you share with them; also happy to communicate with them directly if they like. If there is anything I can do to help, please let me know…

I should also point out that even when the timeout occurs, it is purely a network failure between the client and the CodinGame server (in the Cloudflare load balancer). The CodinGame server is unaware of the failure and continues to run the updateContribution request to completion. If the request succeeds, a subsequent refresh on the contribution page (or a findContribution API request at the protocol level) will show that the contribution did indeed update correctly.  In my own code I have worked around the timeout by detecting it and falling back to polling with findContribution to determine when the update finished and to get the final results.

Thanks. That also matches what I've observed a few times: after a timeout, refreshing the page later sometimes shows that the update actually succeeded. One question: are you confident the timeout is specifically happening in the Cloudflare load balancer, or was that just your best guess based on the observed behaviour? I just want to make sure I don't present speculation as fact when I relay this to the CG team.

Almost certainly coming from Cloudflare load balancer. It is returning HTTP status code 524, which is a Cloudflare-specific timeout error code (though nothing stops someone from reusing it, and there would be no way for me to know for sure):

https://developers.cloudflare.com/support/troubleshooting/http-status-codes/cloudflare-5xx-errors/error-524/

Thanks. I think that could work, but a few things come to mind.

The current (unrevised) Goal section is already around 4.2k characters, with a 5k limit. So, the feasibility of adding timestamps will depend on how much additional explanation is needed.

From a puzzle-design perspective, differentiating it from existing dependency-graph-style puzzles is not a bad idea, given that there's already a somewhat similar puzzle involving library dependencies, cycle detection, and lexicographic tie-breaking/reordering (see https://www.codingame.com/training/easy/library-dependencies ).

That said, it depends on the complexity level you're aiming for. Adding timestamps could make the puzzle more interesting and make the puzzle a closer simulation of make-style build behaviour, but it'd also move the puzzle away from being a relatively straightforward graph problem and increase both implementation and statement complexity.
